VENGEANCE.
Terrible Condition of Affairs in Indian Territory-A Bloody Battle Imminent.
VINITA, I. T., August 3.—On the 26th of July two Creek negro cattle thieves, named Manlay and Jones, were hanged near Gibson Station, Creek Nation, it is supposed by Texas cattle men, who had lost sixteen cattle while driving through that neighborhood. This seems to have aroused the colored men of the Creek Nation, who accused the Cherokees of hanging the thieves. On Tuesday morning thirteen negroes crossed into the Cherokee side, swearing they would kill the first Cherokee they met. Two Cherokee boys named Cobb and Cowan, who had been to Gilson, returning home were met by these black devils and fired upon. Cowan was badly wounded in the face, and his horse became frightened and ran away, carrying him out of their reach.

Young Cobb showed fight, and leaping off his horse began returning the fire, falling back as fast as he emptied his revolver, loading as he ran toward his uncle's house, a mile away, but was shot down when near the house, and died in three hours.

The Cherokees are greatly incensed, and have demanded the thirteen negroes of the Creek Chief, giving him until tonight to surrender them, when, if they are not given up, they declare they will go after them.

The Creeks are said to be willing to surrender the negroes, but it is thought they will not be able to do so, the negroes being too strong for them.

It was difficult for Chiefs Bushyhead and Adair to restrain the Cherokees from immediate vengeance, and they will be unable to keep them off the Creek territory longer than to-morrow morning.

THE CREEK-CHEROKEE TROUBLES.
MUSICOGRAPH L T AUG 4. The Cree
THE CREEK-CHEROKEE TROUBLES.
MUSKOGEE, I. T., August 4.—The Creek-Cherokee council adjourned this afternoon. The result of their deliberation has not been made known, but the following is reliable: The Creeks have agreed to arrest the murderers of Cobb, wherever found, in their jurisdiction. A joint commission, two Creek and two Cherokees, will survey the ground and ascertain whether Cobb killed on Cherokee or Creek soil. If on the former, the murderers will be surrendered to the Cherokees for trial; if on Creek soil, the Creeks will try them. The Cherokees will disband and go home to await the decision of the commission. All trouble is at an end for the present. None of the murderers have yet been arrested, but will be as soon as they show themselves.
dick-glass-fort-gibson-1880-08-04.A9:
Trouble Among the Cherokee
LITTLE ROCK ARK Aug 6
Trouble Among the Cherokees and Creeks.
LITTLE Rock, Ark., Aug. 6.—Reports are received from Fort Smith of serious trouble at Muscogee Creek nation between Creek negroes and Cherokees. Two Creek negro horse thieves, Bill Peters and Long Monday, were hanged by Cherokee lynchers on the 27th ult. On Wednesday, the 13th, Creek negroes crossed into the Cherokee nation and shot two young Cherokees, Wm. Cobb and Alex. Cowan, the first killed, the latter fatally wounded. Dick Glass, a Creek, was killed also in the fight. At last accounts some 200 Cherokees were assembled at Fort Gibson, near the line, intending to attack the Creek negroes, also in force, only desisting at the interposition of chiefs Brushy Head and Ross, who obtained a promise of suspension of hostilities if the Creek negroes were delivered to the Cherokees by Thursday morning last. A white man was reported killed on Tuesday last, which will require the interference of the federal authorities.

Inner History of the Recent Outbreak in Indian Territory.
Chicago Times Special, from Parsons Kansas; The outbreak in Indion Indian Territory is the result of an animosity which has been brewing between the Cherokee Indians and the Creek negroes for some time. Though the feeling has been very bitter, it is probable they would not have commenced spilling each other's blood as soon as they did had it not been for a few of the negroes belonging to the so-called Black Terror band, which consists of a lot of Creek negroes, banded together ostensibly for the purpose of protecting their rights, but in reality for the purpose of thieving and plundering. They are concealed a few miles below Gibson, in the thick underbrush which is a perfect jungle in the bend of the Arkansas. It appears that the few mentioned had been out on one of their raids and had run off fifteen or eighteen head of cattle belonging to the Cherokees. This was done in the night. The next morning the Cherokees started in pursuit, and about 4 o'clock p.m. came upon the negroes, who had two of the animals butchered, and were making preparations to continue the slaughter. The negroes made their escape, with the exception of two, whom the Cherokees, with the usual quietude of Indians, proceeded to hang, after which they returned to their wigwams. The blacks returned that night to the scene of the attack, and finding their two comrades enjoying a swing, they declared vengeance, and accordingly started out for that purpose. They ran down two Cherokees, whom they proceeded to fill with shot and ball. They did not kill them outright, but both are dead. The Cherokees are very indignant, and declare their intention of driving out every black in the nation. The blacks claim a heritage to the land on the ground that they are part Indians. The Cherokees are gathering at Gibson. The trains pass small bands of them every little ways, armed with axes, corn cutters, etc., going to the rally. Some of the Choctaw negroes are joining the Creek negroes against the Cherokees. The Creek Indians say they hope the Cherokees will drive the blacks out of their country, as it will save them the trouble. The affair will result eventually in the opening up of the territory to white settlement, which should be done.

The Creek Indians wisely conclude to give up the negroes for trial and punishment.
dick-glass-fort-gibson-1880-08-04.A23:
PERSONAL AND GENERAL.
ST. AUBREY C. ANGELO, a correspondent of the Liverpool (Eng.) Courier, who has been making a tour of the West in the interests of that journal, was found dead beside the Union Pacific track, near Laramie City, a few days ago. He had been run over by the cars, and ended his life by shooting himself through the heart. Angelo was with Prince Napoleon in Zululand when the latter was killed, and was a most accomplished and enterprising journalist.

GEN. WEAVER, Presidential nominee of the National Greenback-Labor Party, has issued a circular to members of the party, appealing for contributions of one dollar and upward to aid in defraying the expenses of the campaign from now until November.

FIVE hundred Chicago shoemakers are on a strike.

THE Republicans of Cincinnati have renominated their present Representatives in Congress—Benjamin Butterworth in the First, and Thomas L. Young in the Second District.

A DISPATCH from Indian Territory states that the Cherokee Indians and Creek negroes, recently at war, have negotiated a peace, the Creek Indians acting as mediators.

The rumored filibustering expedition into Mexico is understood to be a part of a plan for declaring the independence of the Northwestern States of Sonora, Chihuahua and Sinaloa, and setting up a Government of their own. The natives are led in the scheme by an ex-Governor of Sonora, and backed by Arizona miners. Certain mining companies are understood to lend financial aid to the movement.

JOHN McGUIRE was hanged at San Rafael, Cal., on the 6th, for the murder of a fellow-convict in the State Penitentiary.

It was reported on the 6th that young Cash, son of Col. Cash, who killed Col. Shannon in a duel recently in South Carolina, had fought a duel with Blair, an editor, in which Cash was killed. The latter is said to have challenged Blair on account of certain strictures published by him on the Cash-Shannon affair.

A SPECIAL to the Dallas Herald from Ennis, Texas, says: R. L. Edwards, a Christian preacher, living near Bristol, was called out of his house and shot dead by unknown parties. No further particulars given.

The wife of Woodson L. Gunnells, a well-to-do farmer living twenty miles west of Americus, Ga., during the absence of her husband compounded a pitcher of lemonade into which she put a quantity of morphia. Herself and ten children—four of her own and six of Mr. Gunnells's by a previous wife—drank freely of this. When Mr. Gunnells returned home he found his entire family completely stupefied. Mrs. Gunnells died in a short time and no hopes were entertained for three of the children. The others will recover. Mrs. Gunnells left a note stating that she had deliberately administered the poison to the children and herself with the intention of destroying them all, but did not give any reason, only stating that it was not on account of domestic trouble.

The New Mexico Republican Territorial Convention nominated Hon. Tranquilino Luna for Delegate to Congress.

HENRY SUSA, a watchman in the Manhattan Vinegar Company's Works in Brooklyn, N. Y., was burned to death on the morning of the 6th by a fire which occurred in the building.

C. B. LOCKWOOD, Congressional candidate of the bolting Republicans in the Cleveland (O.) district, has published a card withdrawing from the canvass in the interests of party harmony.

PIETRO BALBO, the Italian who killed his wife in New York City a year ago, was hanged in the Tombs on the 6th.

A DISPATCH from Los Pinos, Colo., 6th, says the Indian Commission had started for the Southern Ute Agency. Chief Ouray will join the Commission there, to use his influence in securing the adoption of the treaty.

THREE passenger cars on an excursion train returning from Niagara Falls to Jackson, O., via the Springfield Southern Railroad, went through a bridge into the canal at Waverly on the evening of the 6th. The front car jumped the track and went over the bridge, carrying it down and throwing other cars off the track. The locomotive crossed safely. One hundred and fifty passengers, residents of Jackson and vicinity, were on the train. The casualties are: David Dungan, killed; Thomas Dungan, back broken; Mrs. Bertsch, arm broken, and a number of others more or less injured.

REPUBLICAN BULLDOZERS.
THEY LEAVE A NOTE ON THE DOOR STEP OF
A COLORED DEMOCRAT IN WHICH THEY
THREATEN TO TAR AND FEATHER HIM UNLESS HE LEAVES THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY.

Mr. J. T. Allen, one of Cairo's colored Democrats, has, like all other independent colored men of this city, been repeatedly insulted and threatened with bodily injury, since he has given expression to his Democratic convictions. The threats were of daily occurrence, but the colored Democrats were not to be intimidated; they were rather confirmed in their convictions by them and boldly joined the Democratic Roosters' club and turned out with them in procession. This was too much for the Republican hot headed whites as well as blacks, and the sneers and insults which have from that time been daily heaped upon the colored Democrats, have become almost imbearable. But not until Sunday last did these Radicals become sufficiently bold to send Allen a letter in which they threatened to tar and feather him for refusing to be a political tool and daring to give expression to his honest convictions.

Day before yesterday morning as Mr. Allen was leaving his house, he found the letter on his front door step—it evidently having been thrown there the night before by the cowards who wrote it and whose fear of detection prevented them from putting it under the door. After opening and reading it he brought it to us with the following note:

Editor Cairo Bulletin.

You will do me a great favor by publishing the following letter, to show what a free government we are living under. I have been insulted every day, since the campaign opened by, colored men. And threats have been made to my face, that if I did not leave the Democratic party, that I would be roughly handled, but I did not think they would go so far as to send me a notice to that effect, I wish to say to my colored Republicans that threats will never scare me into their corrupt ranks. You might as well stop your blowinfl as I am unmovable.

J. T. ALLEN

The below is the letter, which we present without alteration either in spelling or punctuation, and to which we call the attention of all our readers, irrespective of political creed, and ask them to divest themselves of all party bias and, uninfluenced by any consideration of a political character, read it, ponder over it and say whether such bulldozing shall be tolerated in this county during the present campaign:

Cairo.

to Jim. t. Alen and all other niger democrats if you dont Leav the Roosters an all the rest of the democrats Clubs you shall be taken out of the ranks and taired and fethered and drummed of of town we have put up with your dam foolishness long anuff
j-t-allen-cairo-1880-08-29.A2:
We the collord repubcans have stood it now since ole greenly run for president thinkin you would se your Rong an com to our ranks an as you still stay With the dam Rebbles we as loyal citizens of this city wont allow it any longer. so tak head in time for you shall never vote for Hancock an inglish there is not a nuff democrats in Cairo to have you reman so beware COLLORED REPUBLICAN.

It is unnecessary to say that neither Mr. Allen nor we have any idea who the author of the letter is. It is Mr. Allen's opinion that he is a colored men, but from the handwriting (which is disguised) and several expressions contained in the letter—such as "take heed in time"—we are inclined to believe that the writer is a white man, and if he is, he is certainly the most contemptible of his kind.

Mr. Allen is a quiet, unassuming man who never mentions politics to anybody and pays strict attention to his own affairs His language is always that of a gentleman and he studiously avoids coming in contact with boisterous and quarrelsome characters. It is, therefore, not probable that he should have done or said anything that would have induced anybody to write the above for any other reason than to frighten him back into the Republican party. This is the evident intention of the authors and should they make any further attempt in that direction they will surely have cause to regret it and should themselves be "drummed out of town" by the honest members of both parties. They, and the presence of men like them in the Republican ranks fill the negroes with fear and cause them act as machines and

j-t-allen-cairo-1880-08-29.A3:
J. T. ALLEN.
HE TAKES THE EDITOR OF "SQUIRE COMINGS' ORGAN" (THE NEWS) TO TASK IN HIS PLAIN WAY, AND GETS "THE BEST" OF HIM. Editor Cairo Bulletin:

Once more I must take the trouble to reply to the News, hoping it will be the last time that I will have to reply to anything that penny sheet may say, as I do not wish to have newspaper notoriety. The News says in yesterday's issue that "Mr. J. T. Allen, a specimen of colored Democrat, announces that he is the writer of the letter in yesterday's Bulletin, and as we have only the general report to the contrary we give him the benefit of his denial." Now if I knew which of the specimens Mr. Joy alluded to I would know how to reply. If it was my Democracy he meant I can inform him that I am no sample of Democracy, but a full fledged one in all respects, or if it is my color that he meant, it is true I am be tween black and white, but I think that my principles are a great deal whiter than his, as he has proved himself to be the little end of nothing by attacking me through his dirty sheet without cause. He has not yet seen me and does not know whether I am J. T. Allen or some one else. Now, if I am a Democrat, it is a free country. If I stand in my own light I can blame no one for it, so for God's sake let me alone as long as I attend to my own business. If you mistreat a good dog it will make him worthless and of no account. So I think the News should find something else to give its dozen or two of readers besides the name of J. T. Allen, the uneducated Democratic negro. But it always happens that when a Republican carpetbagger emigrates, his first step is to get before the people; then the next is to get his hands into their pockets and then it is good-bye Mr. Carpetbagger. So now, Mr. Editor, in conclusion, I will say to the News, that all articles that have appeared with my name attached, I am the author of, and the letter signed "Colored Republican" was picked up at my door Sunday morning, and printed just as it was written. Now I hope the News will let me alone and tell us about Joe Robarts & Co., and oblige.

J. T. ALLEN.

Cairo, Ill., Sept. 2d.

SHAMEFUL FRAUDS IN ALABAMA.
How the Bourbons Carried the State-Outrageous Bulldozing and Stuffing.
How the Bourbons Carried the State—Outrageous Bulldozing and Stuffing.

A special dispatch from Montgomery, Ala., dated August 3, says: "A most infamous outrage, one which is a fit illustration to the hypocrisy of the democratic platform, has been committed upon the good people of Alabama, and especially upon those of this county. If the people of the country could be made thoroughly conversant with the facts of the so-called election in this state yesterday they would be satisfied beyond all doubt that it will not do at present to intrust the democratic party with power. In the counties of the state where the large republican majorities lie the county officers elected by republicans at former elections have been forced out of office by one means or another, the most effective having been the passage of a law by the legislature refusing to permit persons to become sureties on official bonds who reside outside the limits of the county where the duties of the office were to be performed. Then by ostracising all democrats or republicans who dared go on a republican official bond, the displacement was completed. The importance of having democratic officers in those counties will be seen when it is understood that the appointment of election inspectors and the general control of elections is in their hands. When the time came to appoint inspectors for the last election the persons elected by the republican committees to represent the republicans at the several polls in these counties were deliberately set aside, and ignorant colored men, who were unable to tell a republican from a democratic ballot, were arbitrarily selected to represent the party. To render these poor, innocent instruments even more heipless, the democratic legislature, at its last session, provided that the ballot should be on plain white paper, and should not be counted if there was any device whatever on it. The result has been that, while the republicans polled a larger vote at this election than at any election for years, they were deliberately counted out by men occupying responsible positions in the world, who think it no offense to steal a vote of a negro or a republican.

The election in this county, which in former years registered republican majorities ranging from 3,000 to 4,000, is a fair sample of the conduct of the election elsewhere. At McGhee's Switch, in this county, the republicans polled about 600 votes and the democrats 50. While the votes were being counted, the candle was turned over and put out and the room left in darkness for several minutes. When the colored republican inspector put out his hand to preserve the ballot-box he found that it was gone. Considerable confusion ensued, and on the candle being relighted it was observed that the box had been filled up with new tickets, and that the old ballots were all over the floor. The colored man protested against the fraud and was driven from the room with curses, and was not permitted again to enter and observe the count. The votes have been returned as giving 450 democratic majority. During the count at this precinct, a military company and a large posse of armed citizens, under the command of a deputy sheriff, appeared at the polling place to protect the inspectors, although no trouble or threats of trouble had occurred at the polls. They were determined to force through their nefarious scheme at all hazards, even to have democratic bayonets at the polls. The above-mentioned republican colored inspector made an affidavit to those facts at Kendall's Beat, where the proportion of republican and democratic votes was the same. At McGhee's, the inspectors deliberately changed the votes in the presence of the ignorant, timid old colored man, who finally detected the inspectors with a large roll of bogus tickets. They then tried to bulldoze him into signing the returns, but he would not do so. I might relate similar experiences at each polling place, in this county, because

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune, MILWAUKEE, Aug. 9.—John Godfrey, a young pressman, in the employ of his uncle, George Godfrey, in this city, and son of one of the most noted ministers in Indiana, eloped last night with Miss Clara Knotek, a Bohemian girl of 10 years. Her parents had opposed the match, wishing to make a match with a young man of their own nationality. They were married late in the night and left for Chicago. STRIKE FOR HIGHER WAGES. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. KINGSTON, Ont., Aug. 9.—This morning about 1 o'clock, when elevating had just begun at the forwarding companies, the shovelers struck for higher wages. GEORGIA.

ATLANTA, Ga., Aug. 9.—The Democratic State Convention adjourned until to-morrow upon the twenty-ninth ballot, which showed no change. Gov. Colquitt lacks twenty votes of two-thirds. It is probable the Convention will adjourn to-morrow without a nomination for Governor and State-House officers. The matter will be referred to the people, with a recommendation from the majority to elect Colquitt in October. All parties will unite upon the Electoral ticket and the platform and candidates of the Cincinnati Convention.

ALABAMA.
Special Dispatch to the Chicago Tribune.

WASHINGTON, D. C., Aug. 9.—The following is an extract from an Alabama letter, written by a gentleman who has held high public position, and is well known here:

Such a grand rally of the Republicans has not been seen since 1808, and such intelligent and systematic effort was never put forth by the colored people since the party was formed; but all to no account. Ballots did not decide the election. The Democrats carried every precinct and box in the country except one precinct, where a tally was kept outside, and the Republicans cast 600 votes and the Democrats fifty. Every strong Republican precinct is made to go Democratic except one. You never saw or heard of such doffs. There has been much excitement all day on the part of the colored people, and we barely escaped bloodshed at several polls because of the apparent attempt of the Democrats to steal the votes. In the strife between the Democrats and Independents in Elmore one man was killed. A prominent Democrat said in my presence to-day that another election could never be held under the present law, and I believe he was right. What ought to be done in the Presidential election?

The following letter from Alabama is from a judicial officer of the United States of high character:

The recent election was a complote farce. The Republicans never have cast a more solid vote. The colored people were enthusiastic, and worked with a will to get every vote out, but they had just as well cast their ballots in the fire as to have placed them in the hands of such election inspectors. There is a great deal of bad blood among the negroes. At McGhee's, where we have at least 700 majority, everything went on quietly until the poll closed, and the negroes being pretty bold, and having a competent colored man by the name of Ananius Oliver to represent them on the Board of Inspectors, the Democratic Inspectors were afraid to undertake to count the negroes out without assistance. So the Deputy Sheriff sent a dispatch to the city for assistance, and the Governor ordered Muj. J. G. Jones, with a detachment of the Montgomery Grays, armed by the United States with Springfield rifles, etc., to proceed to McGehoo's. Jones and his troops hurried forward, and, as soon as he arrived, the counting-out process began. After about 200 votes for Buckly were counted out one of the Democratic inspectors knocked the candles over, and before they were relighted the ballots in the box were changed, and Democratic ballots substituted for Republican. Oliver charged the fraud upon the Democratic inspector, for which he was put out of the room. Had not the military been present they would not have dured to do this. The negroes were armed and determined. I believe this is the first illustration of the policy that the bayonet is not a lit instrument for collecting the votes of freedom.

FRAUDS IN ALABAMA.
conform the statements already made that there was most outrageous fraud practised at the recent election in Alabama. Ex-Governor Wm. H. Smith, of that State, recently appointed United States District-Attorney for Alabama, has written the following letter to Marshall Jewell, Chairman of the National Committee:

The Republicans in this State put forth no candidates for any of the State offices, agreeing to vote for the Greenback candidates for State officers, and Greenback and Independent for county officers. The reason for this was that the leaders of that party pledged themselves that if they succeeded henceforth there should be in Alabama a free ballot and a fair count. By thus voting the Republicans expected to secure a fair count of their votes for Garfield and Arthur in November next. The Democrats knew of this intention of the Republicans to vote the Greenback and Independent tickets, and it alarmed them very much, knowing, as they did, that these elements constituted a large majority of the voters of the State.

By the laws of Alabama, "the Probate Judge, Sheriff and Clerk of the Circuit Court, or any two of them, must, at least thirty days before the holding of any election in their county, appoint three inspectors or election for each place of voting, two of whom shall be members of opposing political parties, if practicable." In most of the counties of the State the Judge of Probate, Sheriff and Clerk are Democrats, or at least two of them are; consequently, it was in their power to carry out the law in good faith or to make use of their power for fraudulent partisan purposes. They did the bitter in every county where they had the power, by selecting such men for inspectors as would do the dirty work necessary to overcome the known majority of Greenbackers, Independents and Republicans. In this (Montgomery) county, where the Republican majority, independent of the Greenback and Independent vote, is at least 3,569, the Sheriff and Clerk of the Circuit Court being Democrats and the clerk being a candidate for reelection and the Sheriff a candidate for Tax Collector, selected the inspectors, utterly disregarding any suggestions of the Judge of Probate, who is a Republican and also a candidate for reelection.

For each voting-place the Clerk and Sheriff selected the Democratic and Republican inspectors, taking care in every material case to select a colored man as Republican inspector, and refusing to accept as Republican inspectors well-known, high-minded, honest white Republicans suggested by the Probate Judge. The Democrats selected for inspectors were in almost every case men of notoriously doubtful character for political honesty, and the colored men, with few exceptions, could neither read nor write. Thus the preparation was made beforehand for the count of the ballots.

It is claimed by the Republicans that the colored men have never voted so solidly since 1808 as at the recent election; that more white men voted against the Democrats than ever before, and far more white men refused to vote than used. Notwithstanding, the Democrats claim to have carried the election in this county by
election; that more white men voted against the Democrats than ever before, and far more white men refused to vote than usual. Notwithstanding, the Democrats claim to have carried the election in this county by about 2,700 majority, and the vote has actually been counted that way. I will illustrate by giving you what I believe to be the facts in relation to counting the votes in Precinct No. 9 in this county, known as McGee's Switch.

At this voting-place the Sheriff and the Clerk, by mistake (I suppose), selected a colored man who can read and write, and who had the nerve to contend for a fair count. This so frustrated the plans for counting that the Democrats had to resort to the means described in this affidavit to collect the ballots. The final count of this voting-place gives to the Democrats 540 votes and to the Republicans 13, as printed in The Montgomery Advertiser of the 8th inst. A colored man by the name of H. A. Draper, as each colored man passed him, was informed how he intended to vote, until he had taken down a list of 132 names. After that he tabled each voter until his list reached 460.

The frauds in every voting-place in this country are just as palpable as in this one, and can be easily proved. The Democrats claim that large numbers of colored men voted the Democratic ticket. The Republicans deny it. Suppose you publish an open letter reciting the frauds as herein mentioned, stating that the Democrats deny their truth, and in order to settle the question whether the Democrats have committed these frauds, or whether the Republicans have had, you propose to the chairman of the Democratic National Committee to send an equal number of trustworthy Republicans and Democrats to investigate the master.

The Republicans can and will get in this county the affidavits of at least 6,000 men who will testify that they voted against the Democrats at the late election. If the Democrats accept your proposition, we will prove the frauds by exhibiting 6,000 men who voted as we say they did. If the Democrats decline your proposition, it will be a tacit admission of the fraud.

DETAILS OF THE FRAUD.

Accompanying the communication is the affidavit of A. Oliver, the colored inspector of elections at McGee's Switch. It sets forth that the election was conducted properly, so far as he was aware, until about noon, when the two Democratic inspectors announced that they were going to dinner, and requested him to go outside so that they could look the doors and go away. This he refused to do, and they finally concluded to allow him to remain, leaving one of their number to keep him company. The polls were closed at 5 o'clock, as the law directs, but the inspectors refused to proceed with the count
at that time, claiming that the law directed them
to wait until 7 p. m. The counting was then
begun. At 9 p. m. 171 votes had been counted out
of 672 which had been polled, and of these 116
were Republican and 55 Democratic. At the
hour named one of the Democratic inspectors pro-
posed that they go out and get something to drink,
and the two Democrats went into the adjoining bar-
room. They returned in a short time, and Dr.
McGee, one of the Democratic inspectors, said:

"Buckley and Jeff. Simmons are running
like ——; this thing must be changed." Then
he knocked the candle over, extinguishing
it. At the same moment the ballot-

Soon after the box was returned to the table,
striking the hand of Oliver as it was brought back.
A light was then procured, and Oliver discovered
that the ballot-box had received a considerable accession to its contents, and that the floor from the
place where the ballot-box had been to the door of
the west room was littered with tickets which were
not there when the light was extinguished. When
Oliver discovered this state of things, he arose and
said:

"Gentlemen, this is an unfair deal, and I will not
stand it."

Dr. McGee said: "We are in the majority, and
will rule. We have let you have it your way all

THE ALABAMA FRAUDS.
The Republican State Committee of Alabama has done timely service in putting upon official record the story of the infamous frauds committed during the recent election in that State in the shape of an address to the country. It is a terrible arraignment of the Bourbon Democracy, showing that there is no safeguard for the ballots cast by the Republican party in Alabama, and that there is not even personal safety for the leaders of the party in conducting an election campaign. It is an exposition of high-handed outrages and unblushingly open frauds which should arouse an indignant protest all over the North, and a demand that the rights of citizens in the South who are not Democrats shall be respected.

The address of the Committee is not confined to generalities, but goes into the details of the frauds committed at the last election. A brief abstract of some of them should prove interesting and instructive reading. At McGehee's Switch, in Montgomery County, the Republicans polled 673 votes by actual count, receiving their votes from one man and polling them so that he could see them,—a precaution that was taken because they expected to be cheated. After the polls were closed, the Republican Inspector was ejected. A militia company from Montgomery drove away the Republicans who were waiting outside to hear the returns. The inspectors, having the field to themselves, then proceeded to the count, and made a return giving the Republicans 193 votes and the Democrats 5401 At Kendall's Beat, in the same county, 544 Republican votes were deposited under similar circumstances. A Republican majority of 475 was reduced to 40, and even this little majority was thrown out by the Board of Supervisors. At Roblson's 580 Republican votes were cast and 50 Democratic. At this poll there was a quarrel between two colored men, whereupon the Democratic Inspectors claimed that it invalidated the election, carried off the ballot-box, and no return at all has been made since. The same thing occurred at Porter's Beat, where the vote was 400 Republican to 50 Democratic. The farce that was played at Old Elam is thus described:

At Old Elam the list of votes showed that 448 Republican votes had been polled to sixteen Democratic. The count proceeded at this place until 200 Republican votes and five Democratic votes had been counted out. At this juncture the candle exploded, and it appeared that no other light could be procured. It was accordingly proposed to Charles Pope, the colored inspector, who had been selected for the position because of his ignorance and stupidity, that all the votes be placed together and sent to town, in lieu of a return, which proposition Pope accepted. This proceeding violated everything, because under this law the Inspectors are required to make the count immediately, and it is upon their return, and not by a count of the

votes, that the Board of Supervisors declare the result. To make the thing safe, however, and to make the injury resulting from their action irreparable, the votes as cast, and all the loose papers and trush in the room, with several hundred ballots of both parties, which had not been voted, were dumped indiscriminately into a bag and sent to the Sheriff's office as the return from Elam.

At Union Academy and Dooley, where the Republicans had clear majorities, the inspectors have reported Democratic majorities larger than the entire male population of either place. In Wilcox County, the Republicans, knowing they would be cheated, did not vote at all. Even with the field all to themselves the Democrats returned five times more votes than there were voters. The same fraud was practiced in Lowndes County, and in Greene County, where the Republican majority is over 2,000, the ballot-box was stolen from the Sheriff's office and the Democratic candidate was declared elected. The Committee's report closes with the following ringing protest:

The truth is, that the people are as much opposed to negro suffrage now as they ever were, and, while professedly accepting the constitutional amendments, do not regard it as an offense morally to take advantage of the fluidity and ignorance of the negro to nullify his vote. It is only upon this theory that participation of otherwise honorable men in these frauds, or acceptance of the results of the franks by men of that character, can be accounted for. While this view may lesson the turpitude of the acts committed, before their own consciences, it does not lessen the fear and distrust which the people of the Nation should feel at the domination of the country by people who can bring themselves to so feel and act. An earnest and a manful struggle for a fair, full, and free election has just ended; the vote of nearly 100,000 true and loyal man has been overthrown by the bold and shameless frauds, that can and will be quarried
just ended: the vote of nearly 100,000 true and loyal man has been overthrown by the bold and shameless frauds, that can and will be guarded against in November, of a few hundred election managers whose consciences and fears are hushed, and whose hopes are excited by the wild, sweet music of the Hebel yell. But "The will can never grind with the water that has passed."

In connection with these outrages the colored people of Alabama are preparing to hold a mass-meeting at Montgomery next month, to devise ways and means to assist each other in getting out of the State, and seeking some place where they can have their rights. The appeal of the Committee says:

We are satisfied, in our own mind, that the majority of the white people of this county, especially the planters, men who know that they cannot cultivate their plantations successfully without colored labor, are opposed to those stupendous frauds alluded to above, and would be willing to give us our political and civil rights, but we are sorry to say that they are powerless, and have no control over the ring of unscrupulous politicians who run rough-shoot over this county. A last chance is given to them and to us, and that will be the next Presidential election in November. We love Alabama, and we would like to stay and die in the land where most of us were born, and where the graves of our ancestors lie; but, after we were made FREE MEN, we love our freedom and our rights more, and are determined, in the most peaceable way, to get them respected, and to be ourselves, and our children, FREE MEN FOR ALL TIME TO COME.

How much longer will these infamous outrages be allowed? How man, times must the story be told before the North will solidify itself, its voters, its influence, and its wealth, and put an Administration into power strong enough to enforce the laws and guarantee the rights of every citizen in the South? There is out one way to overcome the Solid South, and that is by the united vigorous action of a Solid North from now until November.

This shameless and disgraceful action of the county officers foreshadowed very plainly what was to follow on election day.

AT M'GEHEE'S SWITCH.

At McGheehe's Switch, in Montgomery county, the Republicans polled 672 votes by actual count, the Republican voters receiving their tickets from one man, giving him their names and going straight from him to the polling-place, holding their tickets in view to enable him to see that they deposited the same ticket they had received. These precautions were adopted in order that the number of Republican votes polled there on that day might be fixed and ascertained beyond all doubt, because at the precinct for member of Congress two years before their votes had been returned as cast for the Democratic candidate. It is instructive to interject here, parenthetically, that B.E. McGheehe, one of the Democratic inspectors at the former election, and who is at present under indictment in the United States circuit court for "stuffing" the ballot-box on that occasion, was one of the persons chosen as a guardian of the people's ballots at this box at this election. After the election had progressed, without one threatening incident, to its close, at 5 o'clock, the Republican inspector, a colored man, demanded that the votes should be immediately counted as the law directed, but could not persuade the other inspector to join him in the count, first one excuse and then another being offered for the delay. About 6 o'clock a military company from Montgomery, the "Grays," under command of Colonel Jones, commanding the second Alabama militia, appeared upon the grounds, supported by an armed posse of about thirty citizens from Montgomery. The cause of the delay then became apparent. The wretches who were housed
commanding the second Alabama militia, appeared upon the grounds, supported by an armed posse of about thirty citizens from Montgomery. The cause of the delay then became apparent. The wretches who were housed inside, contemplating the villainy they were about to perpetrate, became afraid of the indignation and wrath of the large number of colored men who were quietly waiting on the ground to hear the result of the election, announced, and had sent a report to the city that they were threatened by the colored men and that there was danger of a collision. The governor of the State had thereupon issued his mandate, and mustered his bayonets and and dispatched them with all speed to the assistance of his threatened compatriots. The soldiers took up their station and the count proceeded. The details of the farce enacted here have been before published. After counting 116 Republican and 59 Democratic votes, the candle was accidentally extinguished, the ballot-box disappeared from the table, reappeared, the candle was relighted, the box was discovered to be full of tickets, where it had been only partially full by reason of the diminution caused by those already counted, and large numbers of Republican ballots were scattered all over the room, where before there had been none. The colored inspector, inexperienced though he was, could not mistake the meaning of all this, and timid as he was inexperienced, he yet raised his voice in protest. This was the point to which it had been desired to bring him. The other inspectors and the clerks pretended to be indignant at an "imputation upon their integrity," and resented the same with language of such force, accompanied by demonstrations of such character, that the guilty individual made haste to join his friends outside. After being some what reassured by them, he attempted to again enter the polling-place and resume his duties as inspector, but was met by the statement that as he had voluntarily abandoned his post he could not resume it. The inspectors then proceeded to the count, and made a return giving the Republicans 132 votes and the Democrats 540 votes. There are two singular circumstances in connection with the election at this point, which should be marked down. The first is that, of the first 175 votes taken from the box while the Republican inspector was there, 116 were Republican votes, while of the 500 votes taken from the box after the Republican inspector had abandoned his duty, only 16 were Republican votes. The second is, how 132 colored men were enabled to terrorize 540 Democrats, white and black, at that place, and put them in such deadly fright that they required a military company, uniformed and armed with bayonets, to assist them in collecting the votes of the freemen who voted there on that day.

AT WORK FOR GEN. HANCOCK. THE DEMOCRATIC NEWS FROM ALL PARTS OF THE UNITED STATES.
Unexampled Democratic Fervor in Connecticut—Maine Not Sure for the Republicans—The Republican Hancock Club.

The Democratic State Committee are hard at work, and their rooms in the St. James Hotel show signs of the prosecution of an active canvass. Chairman Fowler of the Executive Committee, and Daniel S. Lamont, its clerk, are busy from early morning until late at night reading and replying to letters from all parts of the State, and answering the inquiries of the hundreds of visitors. In another room many clerks are at work folding and mailing documents. The demand for campaign literature is greater than in any former Presidential canvass. The document most sought is that which contains extracts from Republican newspapers against Garfield at the time of the Credit Mobilier exposure in 1873. The gentlemen who have returned from speaking tours in the interior of the State report that the Democrats are enthusiastic and confident, and that the meetings are largely attended. Horatio Seymour and Senator Francis Kernan will speak in Utica on Wednesday evening next. Gov. Seymour's speech will be circulated as a campaign document.

A few days ago Henry A. Glidden, a member of the Republican State Committee from the Orleans Congressional District, said in a political interview that many Democrats in Orleans County would support Garfeld, and that thirty of these gentlemen lived in the village of Albion. E. Kirke Hart, a Democratic ex-Congressman from that district and resident of Albion, has written the Democratic State Committee in relation to Mr. Glidden's assertion. He says: "If my friend Glidden did say so, it must have been in a moment of enthusiasm, while he was trying to cheer his despondent associates. You can rest assured no defection exists with us. If there be any apathy or defection it is all on the other side. The leaders, the old ringers, and the numerous would-be county officials are in a high state of consternation. They see plainly that the rank and file of their own party are either indifferent or inclined to be against them. The fact is our line is unbroken. We are confidently awaiting the issue, with here and there an accession to our ranks, in the full faith that we shall achieve a victory that will bring permanent peace and complete prosperity to our whole country."

The movement begun two weeks ago to organize the Republicans of this city who intend to vote for Hancock is well under way. Its leaders say that three thousand Republicans have already joined its Assembly district associations. Among the influential members of this organization are Leonard W. Jerome, Gen. Daniel Butterfield, Gen. Patrick H. Jones, Col. A. J. H. Duganne, H. H. Hadley, and Chauncey Schaffer. The headquarters of the organization have been established at 21 West Twenty-fourth street. It is expected that before the close of this week associations will be in operation in every Assembly district, and the central organization completely formed.

Senator Wallace of Pennsylvania, Chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Club, was in town yesterday. He is sanguine of the success of the Democracy in the November election. The advices received by his committee lead him to feel confident of Democratic success in Indiana in October, and to believe that Ohio is by no means a sure State for the Republicans. Senator Wallace had no doubt that the differences in the party in Virginia would be amicably adjusted, and the State made absolutely safe for the Democrats. He was not so sure of the result of the Maine election tomorrow. The Democrats and Greenbackers might carry it, but the chances were that it would go Republican.

Ex-State Senator James Gallagher of Connecticut called at the Democratic National Committee's headquarters last evening. He said the campaign in Connecticut is progressing finely. Hancock clubs are forming in all parts of the State. The eastern part of the State is aroused to a degree entirely beyond the expectations of the most sanguine Democrats. This is especially true of Winlham County, which has been the Republican stronghold for twenty-five years. Hancock clubs have been established in every town and village in the county. A mass meeting held last week in Danielsonville, a manufacturing centre in the town of Killingly, in that county, was attended by 2,400 voters. It was the largest Democratic meeting ever held in that county, and was a surprise to the people of the town. The party leaders in that county are not calling for speakers from other parts of the State, but are making the canvass with their local speakers.

Mr. Gallagher added that the Republicans had given up all hope of carrying the State for Garfield or for their State ticket, and were making their fight for the Legislature in the hope of securing votes enough in that body to elect a Republican United States Senator in the place of Senator Eaton, whose term expires in March, 1881.

Mr. J. G. Shaw, a colored man and the editor of the New York Suffragist, who has been speaking for the Democracy in Indiana, said last evening, in the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee, that the campaign in Indiana looked well. "The Democrats are fully equal to the great emergency," he said. "The people are extremely enthusiastic, and at State headquarters great industry prevails. Mr. W. H. English works incessantly. The Republican campaign is noisy. There is no question that a large number of negroes have been imported into Indiana to vote the Republican ticket. I was in a position to know about this matter. I think that many bona fide colored residents of Indiana will express their opinion of this importation of colored men by voting with the Democrats. The Democratic leaders in the State are sure that their candidates for State offices will be elected in October."

Among other visitors to the committee rooms was Gen. Henry W. Slocum, who has just arrived from Europe. He said: "I had made my plans to remain abroad for at least two years, but changed them on learning of the nomination of Gen. Hancock. I have returned to do what I can to assist in his election. I have too much faith in the good sense of the American people to doubt the result. Gen. Hancock, whom I have known intimately for twenty years, has all the qualities of a good civil administrator. I was not surprised at the ability of the state papers issued by him in New Orleans, as I had long known his devotion to the study of constitutional law, which was always one of his hobbies. I am going to Indiana next week to take part in the canvass with Gen. James McQuade and Col. Cole of Troy."

CRIMINALITIES.
AWFUL PUNISHMENT OF A MISERABLE WRETCH,
J. C, Corlew, an ex-convict, under indictment at Moberly, Mo., for one of the basest crimes known to the law, committed in that city several months ago, upon the wife of a respectable citizen of Centralia, Mo., was shot to death in the streets of the former city, on the 29th, while being conveyed from the jail to the court house, where his trial was to take place. Corlew had been confined for some time past in the Kansas City jail as a precaution against lynching, an attempt having been made, soon after the villain's arrest, by a band of men from Centralia, to inflict summary punishment upon him. As stated above, Corlew was on his way to the court house, in charge of Sheriff Matlock, when the crowd opened fire upon him. At the first fire the doomed wretch was hit, but not hurt enough to disable him. He made a desperate effort for life and dashed into the court room, thinking perhaps that the sacred temple of justice would furnish a refuge. He was followed by three of the mob and shot again. With two bullets in his body, he escaped to the street and fell, but regained his feet and ran, receiving another shot. Still struggling to escape he ran through a dry goods store, into an alley and again into the street, with the slayers at his heels. He finally made his way up stairs over a saloon, and stood at bay, cornered like a rat. The husband of the woman he had outraged followed him and put five more bullets into his body, completing the bloody tragedy by putting his pistol to Corlew's forehead and sending a bullet through his brain. Notwithstanding all of his wounds Corlew lived ten minutes after the last shot was fired. During the horrible affair, the officers of the law seemed paralyzed with terror and made no effort to stop the butchery, although the killing was done so quickly that prevention would have been impossible.

A BLOODY FIGHT AT A CAMP MEETING.

A dispatch from Cincinnati, dated the 26th, says: The colored Baptist camp meeting at Danville, ten miles south of Hillsboro, O., was the scene, on Friday night and Sunday afternoon, of a bloody fight. On Friday night a party of drunken roughs went to the camp about 10 o'clock and began an attack with pistols, clubs and stones. They were repulsed and Wm. Diekman, one of their number, shot through the abdomen. Sunday afternoon, a party, said to number about 200, again attacked the camp, and a most desperate fight followed, ending in breaking up the meeting. It is thought some colored people were killed, but they dispersed so rapidly that the facts could not be gathered. No arrests were made.

A FOUL MURDER UNEARTHED.

Workingmen excavating near the relay depot at East St. Louis, came upon a long box which contained the decomposed remains of a man, whose right arm had been broken, whose throat had been cut, and on whose head there were several wounds. Over a year ago Judge Mayo, a banker at Olney, Ill., disappeared at this depot, and it has always been thought that he was enticed from a night train on some pretext, and murdered for his money. As the body discovered by the laborers is believed to be that of Judge Mayo, his friends have been notified.

A BURGLAR SHOT.

A dispatch from Council Bluffs, dated the 27th, says: At an early hour this morning one of two burglars was shot and killed while attempting to make an entrance into the residence of Hon. D. H. Salomon, on the latter's farm about thirty miles from this city, on the Wabash road. The fatal shot was fired by B. L. Salomon, son of D. H. The name of the dead burglar is not known.

ASSASSINATED.

A dispatch from Yazoo City, Miss., dated the 26th, says: Dr. M. F. Williams, of Mechanicsburg, was assassinated while riding home Saturday night. His horse reached home riderless and search being made the doctor's body was found. A negro was arrested on suspicion and has since confessed his guilt. He says he was paid to kill the doctor.

TWO OF THE NOTORIOUS BENDERS ARRESTED.

A dispatch from Fremont, Neb., dated the 29th, says: Two persons, a man and woman, past middle age, captured near here by Sheriff Gregg, are supposed to be old man Bender and Kate, the notorious murderers of Kansas. Both made a positive confession to-day. They will be held here until parties arrive from Kansas to identify them.

CHOKED HIS ASSAILANT TO DEATH,

John King stoned Paul Smith, a negro, in Correville, a Cincinnati suburb, until the fun became monotonous to the African, who turned and ran. King pursued, pelting the colored man with rocks. Finding that there was no escape, Smith seized his persecutor by the throat and literally choked him to death.

A CATTLE HERDER MURDERED.

A dispatch from Caldwell, Kan., dated

the 26th, says: A horrible murder was committed to-day. At 9 a.m. Chas. Wilson murdered W. H. Stephens, foreman of Maj. Hood's cattle men, thirty miles south of here. The body of the murdered man has just arrived, and the murderer will be here this evening.

THE WINTHROP TRAIN ROBBERS.

A dispatch from St. Joseph, dated the 24, says: The case of Ballard and Brooks, Winthrop train robbers, came up in the circuit court to-day. They waived formal examination, and bail was fixel at $5,000 each. At 7 o'clock this evening bail had not been procured. The case will come up at the September term.

KILLED, A POLICEMAN.

A man named Charley Norton kulled a policeman in Kokomo, Col., near Leadville, on the 23rd, and, soon after being placed in jail, was taken out by a mob and lynched. He admitted just before the boys swung him off that he had murdered three other men, and that the punishment was just.

A YOUNG WIFE ELOPES.

Herman Pitchshe, 56 years old, lived at Sedalia, Mo., with his young wife. She finally eloped with a youthful admirer, taking $2,800, her husband's entire fortune. The old man followed the couple to Chicago, where he learned that they had gone to Europe.

A BANK ROBBED.

A dispatch from Hartford, Conn., dated the 27th, says: Three or four men entered Middleton's savings bank during the absence at dinner of some officials, and engaging the clerks in conversation, accomplices robbed the vault of $8,500.

A FIENDISH CRIME.

Abraham Martin, of Abbeville, S. C., knocked his wife down and then, standing on her as he would on a log, chopped her shoulders and sides into shreds. They had been married thirty-five years, and had fourteen children.

STABBED IN A QUABREL.

Harmon McCoy, living four miles from Acola, Ill., was stabbed and killed by Elisha McCabe, aided by Joel Engle, during a quarrel on the night of the 25th. McCabe escaped, but Engle was arrested.

A CROOKED LICENSE CLERK.

Henry Moorman, the license clerk at Cincinnati, is said to have overcharged for licenses, and pocketed the difference. He will be investigated.

A LOTTERY SWINDLER ABRESTED.

The police of Burlington, Iowa, have arrested a young fellow named D. N. Kratzer for conducting a lottery swindle in that city.

A SAFE ROBBED.

Burglars blew open C. S. Woodworth & Co.'s safe at Marshalltown, Iowa, on the 28th, and secured $4,000 worth of securities.

HANGED BY A MOB.

George Washington, a colored murderer, was recently hanged by a mob, in the backwoods of Tennessee.
